title: Ending the relapsing course of severe mood disorders

concept.text: The proposed innovation is a finite treatment course that leaves people with highly recurrent mood illness well and functioning for years after treatment ends. Success would mean sustained recovery without continuing maintenance treatment, rather than symptom relief that depends on repeated dosing, stimulation, or another ongoing intervention. The central target is durability; rapid onset alone would not establish this capability.

Recurrent major depression provides the clearest evidence-grounded starting point in the supplied material. A depression relapse-prevention meta-analysis documents that psychological interventions reduce relapse hazard, while leaving recurrence as an important clinical problem. Bipolar disorder remains within the intended concept, but its inclusion is a proposed extension: the reviewed evidence does not establish comparable results or treatment gaps for bipolar illness.

This is a clinical outcome target, not a claim that all severe mood disorders share one removable recurrence mechanism. Demonstrating prolonged recovery would not require first identifying such a mechanism, and prolonged recovery alone would not prove that one had been eliminated.

significance.text: Recurrence contributes substantially to the burden of major depression. A treatment that reliably sustains recovery after a finite course would therefore address a central source of disability, beyond improvement during an acute episode. The reviewed meta-analysis establishes the importance of relapse prevention and shows that existing psychological approaches can reduce risk; it does not establish elimination of recurrence.

Conditional impact synthesis: if independently replicated, years of functional recovery without maintenance treatment could substantially change management for the population studied. Direct consequences could include fewer recurrent episodes and less dependence on continuing treatment. Reduced treatment burden, disruption to work and relationships, and demand for repeated clinical care would be downstream possibilities requiring measurement, rather than automatic consequences of an improved symptom score.

The analogy to converting a relapsing illness into a single treatable episode has an important limit. Even very low recurrence over two years would establish durable benefit over that interval, not permanent cure or removal of the biological and psychological causes of recurrence. Extension across diagnoses, severity levels, and patient groups would require additional evidence. Maintenance-dependent benefit remains valuable, but answers a different question from treatment-independent recovery; that distinction does not establish a universal ranking of treatments.

missing_breakthrough.text: The missing capability is a reproducible way to sustain functional recovery in highly recurrent illness after a finite intervention, with sufficiently low subsequent recurrence to change the expected clinical course. The supported psychotherapy evidence demonstrates reduced relapse hazard over 12 months, which motivates this target without proving that every available treatment fails to achieve it. The supplied evidence does not justify the stronger assertion that no treatment removes a known, singular recurrence mechanism.

Scientific and engineering synthesis: an intervention would need to produce changes that persist after its active administration ends and remain effective under the conditions in which episodes recur. Development must distinguish a lasting change in illness course from temporary suppression of symptoms, benefit maintained by background treatment, or selection of unusually durable responders. The supplied material does not identify a validated mechanism or intervention that solves these problems.

Demonstration also presents a practical barrier. Long follow-up must capture new episodes, sustained functioning, additional treatment, and participants lost to observation. Studies must distinguish major depression from bipolar disorder and define whether success applies to all enrolled patients or only initial responders. Otherwise, apparently durable benefit could reflect a narrowed sample or unmeasured continuing care rather than the proposed capability.

current_state.text: A 2024 individual-participant meta-analysis of 14 depression relapse-prevention trials, involving 1,720 participants, reported a relapse hazard ratio of 0.60 with a 95 percent confidence interval of 0.48–0.74 for psychological interventions versus non-psychological control conditions. This corresponds to a lower relapse hazard, not a 40-percentage-point absolute reduction in recurrence or elimination of relapse. The reviewed discussion also describes benefit from adding psychological intervention to treatment as usual during recovery or remission, so the result does not establish recovery without continuing care.

Follow-up in that meta-analysis was censored at 12 months, limiting conclusions about longer-term durability; the authors recommended longer follow-up. The supplied review found the relevant methods, results, and discussion readable in an identifiable article, but treated the extracted PDF as partial because pages 11–13 lacked extractable text and an extraction warning was present. Those limitations do not invalidate the readable estimate, but they limit claims about complete inspection of the paper.

The earlier research attributes to a July 2025 Stanford Neuromodulation Therapy follow-up a 12-week remission rate of 32.6 percent, or 15 of 46 participants with follow-up, and a response rate of 37.0 percent. These figures are preserved as research-reported findings: no article or abstract text from this source was retained for the supplied evidence review, so their accuracy, denominators, and follow-up context could not be checked there. The reported endpoint rates alone would also be insufficient to establish how much initial remission was lost without the baseline remission count and participant flow.

The research separately describes a January 2025 open-label continuation pilot involving 21 responders whose remission was reportedly maintained through further stimulation courses when symptoms worsened. No source text was retained for review, leaving the numerical and procedural details unverified here. If that description is accurate, it concerns maintenance through retreatment, rather than recovery sustained after treatment has ended; the uncontrolled responder sample would also limit causal and population-wide conclusions.

For the 2019 SUSTAIN-1 randomized withdrawal trial, the research reports relapse in 26.7 percent of adults in stable remission who continued esketamine plus an oral antidepressant, versus 45.3 percent of those switched to placebo nasal spray while continuing the oral antidepressant. The supplied review had no retained article text with which to verify these figures or their detailed context. As described, the trial tests continuation of esketamine among selected patients who had reached stable remission, with oral antidepressant treatment in both groups. It would support delayed relapse during continued treatment, rather than treatment-independent recovery or abolition of recurrence.

The research attributes to a November 2022 systematic review the summary that benefits after a single ketamine dose usually disappear within two weeks and that median time to relapse after cessation of repeated dosing remains about two to three weeks. It identifies this as an introductory summary citing earlier studies, not a new pooled estimate. No source text was retained for the supplied review, and the original research did not download the full PDF; these duration claims therefore remain unverified in this record and should not be generalized to every regimen or patient. The broader assertion that rapid ketamine benefit is already demonstrated likewise was not independently established by the retained evidence.

The earlier research describes company topline reports for COMP360 psilocybin as showing six-week MADRS advantages of approximately 3.6–3.8 points. Its description of the October 30, 2026 COMP006 news report gives a 3.8-point advantage and a reduction of at least 25 percent in 39 percent of participants. These details remain unresolved: the retained page contained only a loading challenge, so the review could not identify article content or verify the figures, response definition, or reporting context. A 25 percent symptom-reduction threshold, if confirmed, must be distinguished from remission, conventional response definitions, and prevention of later episodes.

The research characterizes those psilocybin findings as company reports rather than a peer-reviewed trial publication. However, the supplied materials contain no bounded search record establishing that a peer-reviewed report was absent, and they do not substantiate the claimed incomplete rolling FDA submission in late 2026. Publication status, submission status, approval status, and long-term recurrence outcomes cannot be resolved from the inaccessible news content. Missing evidence is not evidence that the reported trial results are false.

An identifiable August 12, 2026 Psychedelic Alpha article reports an MDMA-for-PTSD resubmission following an earlier FDA rejection and describes approval as pending at that time. This is secondary journalism, with filing information attributed to anonymous sources. It does not establish the precise rejection month or continued nonapproval through October 2026; later sidebar headlines do not update the article's regulatory account. PTSD treatment is peripheral to this mood-disorder concept, and its regulatory history does not establish durability in major depression or bipolar disorder.

The supplied evidence does not establish a comprehensive treatment or regulatory picture as of November 1, 2026. Retrieval dates establish when material was collected, not that a systematic search captured all relevant developments. The evidence-grounded conclusion is narrower: relapse-risk reduction is documented in the reviewed depression meta-analysis, while the proposed capability of replicated, prolonged recovery without maintenance treatment is not demonstrated by the supplied materials.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed demonstration: conduct a pre-registered, adequately powered controlled trial in a clearly defined population with highly recurrent major depression or bipolar disorder, followed by independent replication. Deliver a time-limited intervention and follow participants for at least two years after it ends. Two years is a proposed threshold for convincing durability, not an established consensus standard. A trial in one diagnosis would establish evidence for that diagnosis and population, rather than for all severe mood disorders.
completion_criteria.label: Independently replicated controlled trials include at least two-year post-treatment follow-up

completion_criteria.text: Pre-specify both a low absolute recurrence rate and a clinically substantial reduction versus a concurrent control, together with sustained functional recovery. Define what counts as recurrence, the acceptable rate, uncertainty bounds, sample size, and handling of attrition before results are known. Historical expectations can help interpret the population's illness course, but should not replace the concurrent comparison. Repeated symptom assessments should support episode ascertainment, while functional outcomes establish whether participants remain meaningfully well.
completion_criteria.label: Low recurrence substantially below concurrent controls accompanies sustained functional recovery

completion_criteria.text: Align the treatment claim with background care. Remaining off only the investigational intervention would demonstrate durability after that intervention under the accompanying care conditions. The stronger claim of recovery without continuous treatment requires demonstrating the result without ongoing maintenance medication, stimulation, or other relapse-prevention treatment, with appropriate clinical safeguards. Rescue treatment must remain available and be recorded and handled explicitly in the outcome analysis; its use cannot silently count as treatment-independent recovery.
completion_criteria.label: Recovery claims reflect background maintenance care and rescue-treatment use

completion_criteria.text: Replication should establish whether benefit extends beyond a selected group of initial responders and across relevant clinical settings. Report adverse outcomes and the boundaries within which foregoing maintenance treatment was studied. Ongoing stimulation, continuing medication, repeated rescue courses, or a short-term symptom-score advantage alone would not meet the stronger proposed criterion. Rapid onset is optional because durability is the target. Even successful finite trials would establish demonstrated breadth and duration, not permanent cure or universal protection from recurrence.
completion_criteria.label: Replication establishes benefit breadth, adverse outcomes, and maintenance-free recovery limits

related_concepts.text: Roster-based synthesis: PSY-12, “A session-level amplifier that lets brief psychotherapy match a full course,” concerns treatment efficiency, whereas PSY-03 concerns subsequent illness course. A brief course could match a longer course without preventing later episodes. One intervention could satisfy both concepts if it also produced replicated, durable recovery after treatment ended; the entries remain distinct.

Roster-based synthesis: PSY-01, “Mechanism-defined diseases in place of the major syndromes,” and PSY-05, “Medicines designed from a confirmed human disease mechanism,” could help identify responsive subgroups or develop finite interventions. PSY-03 instead defines success through clinical durability. It neither requires those mechanistic advances nor establishes them merely by showing prolonged recovery.

Roster-based synthesis: PSY-06, “A clinical instrument that reads an individual’s psychiatric state,” could improve monitoring and recurrence detection. PSY-07, “Reliable causal control of a core symptom by a defined circuit,” could supply an intervention target. Measuring state or controlling a symptom does not by itself establish multi-year functional recovery after treatment ceases.

Roster-based synthesis: PSY-08, “Selective and durable modification of a pathological memory,” and PSY-10, “Reopening plasticity that can repair an established psychiatric deficit,” describe possible routes to lasting change. Neither a durable memory modification nor increased capacity for learning establishes prevention of recurrent mood episodes without direct clinical evidence. PSY-03 remains the illness-course outcome, rather than a particular memory or plasticity mechanism.

Roster-based synthesis: PSY-02, “A treatment that changes the course of schizophrenia,” and PSY-09, “A time-limited reset of severe addiction,” share the ambition of changing a disorder's trajectory. Their diagnoses, outcomes, and recurrence patterns differ. Success in schizophrenia or addiction would not establish the mood-disorder capability, and success in major depression would not establish either neighboring concept.

Roster-based synthesis: PSY-04, “Primary prevention that lowers incidence of a major disorder,” concerns preventing initial onset. PSY-11, “Prevention of post-traumatic stress disorder by blocking consolidation,” concerns prevention following trauma through a specified process. PSY-03 concerns recurrence after established mood illness. These prevention goals can share methods or biological insights while retaining different populations and endpoints; MDMA treatment of established PTSD does not itself demonstrate either prevention concept.

change_log.change: Preserved PSY-03's identity and centered its explanation on sustained functional recovery after finite treatment.
change_log.reason: The clinically meaningful innovation survives uncertainty about individual supporting treatment claims.

change_log.change: Replaced the assertion that no treatment removes a recurrence mechanism with a bounded clinical capability gap.
change_log.reason: The reviewed evidence does not establish a universal treatment failure or a single removable mechanism.

change_log.change: Retained bipolar disorder as intended scope while separating it from the depression evidence.
change_log.reason: The reviewed scientific evidence concerns major depression and does not establish bipolar generalization.

change_log.change: Integrated the meta-analysis population, comparator, hazard interpretation, 12-month censoring, and partial extraction limitations.
change_log.reason: These details distinguish documented relapse-risk reduction from absolute risk reduction, treatment independence, or permanent cure.

change_log.change: Preserved research-reported stimulation, esketamine, ketamine, and psilocybin quantities with explicit verification limits.
change_log.reason: The user requested quantitative preservation where unresolved. Missing retained evidence warrants qualification rather than deletion or a finding of falsity.

change_log.change: Removed the inference that the reported stimulation endpoint alone proves loss of most initial remission.
change_log.reason: That conclusion requires initial remission counts and participant-flow information absent from the supplied review.

change_log.change: Separated maintenance findings, selected-responder designs, symptom improvement, remission, and recurrence prevention.
change_log.reason: These outcomes and study populations support different conclusions about durability.

change_log.change: Qualified psilocybin publication, submission, and approval assertions, and limited MDMA regulatory reporting to its August 2026 context.
change_log.reason: The psilocybin artifact contained no article content, and the MDMA article did not establish later regulatory status.

change_log.change: Replaced permanent conversion to a single episode with conditional, time-bounded clinical impact.
change_log.reason: Finite follow-up cannot establish permanent cure or removal of recurrence mechanisms.

change_log.change: Aligned completion criteria with the stronger claim of recovery without maintenance treatment and operationalized recurrence assessment.
change_log.reason: Stopping only the investigational treatment supports a narrower conclusion; concurrent controls, uncertainty bounds, rescue care, and replication make the proposal interpretable.

change_log.change: Used the supplied roster to explain PSY-12 and the other neighboring concepts while preserving every entry.
change_log.reason: Although the review lacked an independent PSY-12 definition, the supplied roster explicitly provides its title and permits a bounded conceptual distinction.

unresolved_issues: The stimulation, SUSTAIN-1, and ketamine sources lack retained text for review; their research-reported quantities and contextual details remain unverified.
The psilocybin page retained only a loading challenge. Trial figures, response definitions, publication status, regulatory status, and durable recurrence outcomes remain unresolved.
A comprehensive treatment and regulatory assessment as of November 1, 2026 cannot be reconstructed from the supplied search record.
The supplied materials do not establish the proposed treatment gap or a finite-treatment solution in bipolar disorder.
No exact acceptable recurrence rate, functional recovery threshold, uncertainty bound, or replication design has been selected for the proposed completion criteria.
The practical and clinical boundaries for demonstrating recovery without maintenance treatment remain to be specified, including rescue care and safe participation.

The review's recommendation to omit unverifiable treatment-specific numbers was not adopted wholesale: the numbers were retained as explicitly qualified research reports to satisfy the requested preservation of unresolved quantitative detail.
The review's caution about PSY-12's undefined scope was resolved only to the extent permitted by the supplied roster title; no additional mechanism or evidence was inferred.

brief.title: Lasting recovery after mood disorder treatment ends
possible: People whose severe mood illness keeps returning could finish a course of treatment and stay well for years. They could sustain daily life without continuing medication, brain stimulation or other treatment to prevent new episodes.
why: Repeated episodes of depression are a major source of disability. Lasting recovery could mean fewer episodes and less dependence on continuing treatment. It could also reduce disruption to work and relationships and the need for repeated clinical care.

sources.who: Josefien J. F. Breedvelt and colleagues
sources.showed: Their combined analysis of depression trials found that psychological therapies delayed relapse, meaning the return of depression. People with more previous episodes benefited more.
sources.quote:
The number of previous depression 
episodes moderated the treatment effect, with psychological interventions 
demonstrating greater efficacy for patients with three or more previous 
episodes.
sources.cited_for: Psychological therapies can reduce the risk of depression returning.
sources.not_established: The analysis did not establish years of recovery after all continuing treatment ends.

sources.showed: This follow-up study examined how long benefits lasted after a course of brain stimulation.
sources.cited_for: The study addresses whether benefits persist after stimulation ends.
sources.not_established: Short follow-up does not establish years of sustained recovery.

sources.who: Researchers studying the Magnus Neuromodulation System
sources.showed: This small, uncontrolled pilot studied further brain stimulation when symptoms worsened in people who had already benefited.
sources.cited_for: The pilot concerns maintaining benefit through repeated treatment.
sources.not_established: Repeated stimulation does not establish recovery after treatment ends, and selected responders may not represent everyone.

sources.showed: This trial compared continuing esketamine nasal spray with switching to an inactive spray while both groups continued an oral antidepressant.
sources.cited_for: The trial addresses preventing depression from returning during continued treatment.
sources.not_established: Continuing antidepressant treatment in both groups prevents a claim of recovery without ongoing treatment.

sources.showed: This systematic review examined the effectiveness, safety and tolerability of continuing ketamine treatment for depression.
sources.cited_for: The review concerns how ketamine benefits are maintained.
sources.not_established: It does not establish reliable, prolonged recovery after a finite course.

sources.showed: This news report describes company announcements of short-term depression symptom results for psilocybin, a psychedelic drug.
sources.cited_for: The report concerns symptom improvement during a depression trial.
sources.not_established: Short-term symptom improvement does not establish sustained recovery or prevention of later episodes.

sources.showed: Hardman reported, citing anonymous sources, that Resilient Pharmaceuticals had resubmitted its application for MDMA treatment of post-traumatic stress disorder, a trauma-related condition.
sources.cited_for: The article provides regulatory context for a psychedelic treatment of a different condition.
sources.not_established: An application for approval does not establish lasting recovery in depression or bipolar disorder.

shown: Breedvelt and colleagues found that psychological therapies reduced the risk of depression returning over 12 months. This is the clearest demonstrated progress toward preventing repeated episodes.
missing: A finite treatment must reproducibly leave people well and functioning for years after it ends.
Controlled trials must establish recovery without continuing treatment to prevent new episodes.
Long follow-up must track new episodes, daily functioning, additional treatment and people who leave the study.

milestones.label: Independent trials confirm recovery over two years after treatment
milestones.explanation: Controlled trials in a clearly defined group would have to follow patients for at least two years after treatment, with independent replication. This would establish durability in that group.

milestones.label: Low recurrence accompanies sustained daily functioning
milestones.explanation: Trials would have to show few new episodes, substantially fewer than in a concurrent comparison group, alongside sustained daily functioning. This would distinguish lasting recovery from a temporary improvement in symptoms.

milestones.label: Recovery persists without continuing preventive treatment
milestones.explanation: Trials would have to account for all continuing care and treatment given when symptoms worsen. This would establish whether recovery persists without ongoing treatment to prevent new episodes.

milestones.label: Replication establishes who benefits and the limits of recovery
milestones.explanation: Independent studies would have to test benefit beyond selected early responders, across care settings, and report harms. This would establish who can recover without continuing treatment and for how long.

uncertain: The acceptable rate of new episodes and the threshold for sustained daily functioning remain to be defined.
Whether comparable results could extend to bipolar disorder remains open.
Even years of recovery would not establish a permanent cure or removal of the causes of recurring illness.
